Title: Library of Ashurbanipal
Description: Fragment from the right half of a clay tablet, 17 lines of inscription. Neo-Assyrian. A manuscript of chapter 2 of the treatise addressing conditions affecting the neck, as part of the Nineveh Medical Encyclopaedia.;
Inscription:
Inscription type: inscription Inscription script: cuneiform Inscription translation: (o 1) . . . urânu-plant (‘anise’), zalāqu-stone (‘shiny’ stone) (and) nikiptu-aromatic (‘spurge’) in a leather bag.
(o 2) . . . the head(?) of a fly in a leather bag, (and) you put it on his neck.
(o 3–o 4) . . . which has not yet seen . . . hair from an unmated female kid . . . in a leather bag, (and) you put it on his neck.
(o 5) . . . hair from the tail of a dog in a leather bag.
(o 6) If a ghost has settled on someone: . . . tooth(?) from a dog (and) mūṣu-stone in a leather bag.
(o 7) If DITTO, you mix mūṣu-stone, hair from a monkey, nikiptu-aromatic (‘spurge’) (and) azukirānu-plant (‘saffron’) with fat from a man, (and) you anoint him with it in oil from serdu-tree (‘olive’).
(o 8–o 9) If DITTO, mūṣu-stone, nikiptu-aromatic (‘spurge’), powder from the . . . of a copper statue, cuttings from ēru-tree (and) hair from an unmated black and white lamb in a leather bag (dipped) in milk, (and then) you fumigate him with . . . (and) hair from an unmated female kid.
(o 10–o 12) If DITTO, kibrītu (a kind of sulphur), atā’išu-plant, nikiptu-aromatic (‘spurge’), stag horn, fragment of a human skull, resin from abukkatu-tree, fat from the left kidney of a black ox, sīḫu-tree (‘wormwood’), argannu-tree (‘conifer’), barīrātu-tree (‘sagapenum’), gazelle droppings, gazelle meat, human flesh (and) emesallu salt (gloss: kupad salt)—altogether fourteen drugs for a fumigation against ‘hand-of-ghost’.
(o 13–o 15) tarmuš-plant (‘lupin’), imḫur-līm-plant (‘faces a thousand’ plant), imḫur-ešrā-plant (‘faces twenty’ plant), atā’išu-plant, ṭūru-aromatic (‘opopanax’), murru-aromatic (‘myrrh’), gazelle skin, lapat armanni-plant (‘armannu-like turnip’), imbū tâmti (‘algae’), shoots from grain, uḫūlu qarnānû (‘horned alkali’), šūmū(?)-herb (‘garlic’), burāšu-aromatic (a kind of juniper), fat from the kidney of an old ox—you mix these fourteen drugs in sap from erēnu-tree (‘cedar’) together, (and you fumigate him) over embers.
(o 16–o 17) sīḫu-plant (‘wormwood’), ṣaṣumtu-plant, nīnû-plant (‘mint’), azupīru-plant (‘saffron’), imḫur-līm-plant (‘faces a thousand’ plant), imḫur-ešrā-plant (‘faces twenty’ plant), šumuttu-plant (‘beetroot’)—altogether seven drugs for a fumigation against ‘hand-of-ghost’.;

Title: The Flood Tablet; The Gilgamesh Tablet; Library of Ashurbanipal
Description: Fragment of a clay tablet, upper right corner, 2 columns of inscription on either side, 49 and 51 lines + 45 and 49 lines. Neo-Assyrian. Epic of Gilgamesh, tablet 11, story of the Flood.;
Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription script: cuneiform;
Curators Comments:
This object is the single most famous cuneiform text and caused a sensation when its content was first read in the 19th century because of its similarity to the Flood story in the Book of Genesis. Baked clay tablet inscribed with the Babylonian account of the Flood. 
It is the 11th Tablet of the Epic of Gilgamesh and tells how the gods determined to send a flood to destroy the earth, but one of them, Ea, revealed the plan to Utu-napishtim whom he instructed to make a boat in which to save himself and his family. He orders him to take into it birds and beasts of all kinds. Utu-napishtim obeyed and when all were aboard and the door shut the rains descended and all the rest of mankind perished. After six days the waters abated and the ship grounded. The first bird released "flew to and fro but found no resting-place". A swallow likewise returned but finally a raven which had been sent out did not return showing that the waters were receding. Utu-napishtim, who later told this story to Gilgamesh, thereupon emerged and sacrificed to the gods who, angry at his escape, granted him on the intercession of Ea divine honours and a dwelling place at the mouth of the river Euphrates.
This object was previously moulded by the BM Facsimile Service. It was issued as No. 10 in a previously issued series of postcards captioned "Assyrian monuments bearing on Bible history in the British Museum".

Title: Library of Ashurbanipal
Description: Clay tablet: containing a dated private contract for an exchange of slaves written in 14 + 4 + 18 lines of Neo-Assyrian  inscription, and 1 line in Aramaic. Between lines 5 and 6 the tablet has been impressed three times  sideways with a scaraboid  seal, between ruled lines, and on the left hand margin 1 line with Phoenician characters. The seal has an Egyptianising motif within a line border. A seated god holds the symbol for 'years', meaning 'millions of years'; beneath it is a basket; above is a highly stylised version of the winged sun-disc, or perhaps a disc with uraei.;
Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: face Inscription language: Neo-Assyrian Inscription script: cuneiform Inscription note: Three people, two of whom are brothers, give their male slave, Ishtar-dur-qali, to Kakkullanu,   an army commander, in exchange for his slave-girl, Abi-lihya. Date: 20th Ayaru, eponymy of Sin-sharru-usur. There were eleven witnesses.; Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: face Inscription language: Aramaic Inscription translation: Sale document of Ishtar-dur-qali. Inscription note: It is likely that this note was intended to assist record-keepers who could not read the cuneiform script.;
Curators Comments:
See Smith, G., 1878. 'The Assyrian Eponym Canon'. London: S. Bagster and Sons, p. 97; Strassmaier, J. N. 1882-1886. ‘Alphabetisches Verzeichniss der assyrischen und akkadischen Wörter: der Cuneiform inscriptions of western Asia, vol. II ; sowie anderer meist unveröffentlichter Inschriften / von J.N. Strassmaier ; Mit zahlreichen engänzungen und verbesserungen und einem Wörterverzeichniss zu den in den Verhandlungen’. Leipzig: J.C. Hinrichs, p. 976; and 'Guide to the Kouyunjik Gallery', 1885, p. 175 f, No. 46. For a parallel to the Egyptian seal impression, see Pierre Meyrat, "Un corpus d’empreintes de sceaux de Doukki Gel",
Bulletin de l’Institut français d’archéologie orientale 123, 2023, p. 346 with n. 49 and 50.
